Framing arithmetic that needs no outside data (my own numbers, not evidence): ESTIMATE: $5,000 net per month / (5 working days x 4.33 weeks = 21.65 days) = about $231 net per working day.

ESTIMATE of billable hours for $5,000 net per month: at $25/h net, 5000/25 = 200 h per month, and 200/4.33 = about 46 h per week. At $40/h net, 5000/40 = 125 h per month, about 29 h per week. At $75/h net, 5000/75 = about 67 h per month, about 15 h per week. Paid hours only; unpaid time spent selling, quoting and travelling comes on top.

ESTIMATE of sales volume for $5,000 net per month: at $20 net per sale, 5000/20 = 250 sales. At $150 net per job, 5000/150 = about 33 jobs (about 7.7 per week). At $500 net per job, 10 jobs. At $2,000 net per engagement, 2.5 engagements. From arithmetic alone, a low-ticket product needs hundreds of buyers in month 1, which usually assumes an existing audience or traffic. A local service needs tens of customers, and a high-ticket service needs only a few.

HYPOTHESIS (not supported by evidence gathered here; must be verified before anyone relies on it): the business types most likely to fit a 30-60 day ramp are local, in-person services with high tickets or pre-paid contracts that can be sold directly (door-to-door, neighbourhood groups, the owner's existing network), rather than audience-dependent digital products or new freelance-platform profiles. I could not confirm this with base-rate data, so treat it as a lead, not a finding.

Any guru or 'sweaty startup' income claims (for example, from social media personalities) used downstream should be labelled guru or anecdotal claims and kept apart from survey or government data. None were collected in this run.
